solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Field study for second degree

parts.note: to do a subject is to study it
a Master of Arts, the degree after a BA
the subject you take a degree for is the one it is in

explanation.surface: Someone choosing fieldwork as the research for a master's.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the wordplay as a phrase: to 'do an MA in' history is to study for a second degree.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: your field of expertise is your domain, the area you rule over.

clue.text: Levant PM unable to contact service to north

indicators.note: in a down clue, going north means reading upwards

parts.note: a player who is aced cannot get a racket to the serve

explanation.surface: A Middle Eastern prime minister cut off from the military, somewhere to the north.
explanation.walkthrough: Levant looks like the eastern Mediterranean region, but it is a verb here: to levant is to run off leaving debts unpaid. The service is a tennis serve, not the armed forces.
explanation.definitionFit: To levant and to decamp both mean to leave suddenly or secretly.

clue.text: Million nuts that must be shelled tomorrow

indicators.note: shelling removes the outer layer, here the first and last letters

parts.note: BANANAS (nuts, mad) without its outer letters

explanation.surface: A huge order of nuts whose shells have to come off by tomorrow.
explanation.walkthrough: The nuts are not something to crack: 'bananas' means crazy, and it is the word that gets shelled.
explanation.definitionFit: Mañana is Spanish for tomorrow, used in English for putting things off.

clue.text: Very soon desert old lover

parts.note: to rat is to desert your side

explanation.surface: A warning that you are about to walk out on a former partner.
explanation.walkthrough: Desert is a verb, not sand. 'In a mo' is British slang for 'in a moment'.
explanation.definitionFit: A literary loan from Italian, where the word means 'enamoured', applied to a man in love.

clue.text: Mince on side of skewers almost resembling kebab

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word stops one letter short of its end
the side of a word is its edge, here the first letter

explanation.surface: Minced meat pushed onto skewers until it looks like a kebab.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue sits in the kitchen, so kebab reads as part of the recipe rather than the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Shashlik is a kebab of meat grilled on a skewer.

clue.text: Weed covering allotment alas, mown regularly for war hero

indicators.note: something covering another lies over it on both sides, so one word wraps round the other

parts.note: a ration is an allotted share

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so only every second letter is kept

explanation.surface: A gardener lamenting weeds overrunning an allotment that is only mown now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: An allotment in Britain is a rented garden plot, which is what the surface wants, but here it means a ration.
explanation.definitionFit: Horatio Nelson was the British admiral who won at Trafalgar.

clue.text: Back in Wetherspoons, groom curtailed binge

indicators.note: the back of a word is its last letter
cut off at the tail: drop the last letter

explanation.surface: A bridegroom cut short in a cheap pub during a drinking session.
explanation.walkthrough: Wetherspoons is a chain of cheap British pubs. Groom is the verb, to preen, not a bridegroom.
explanation.definitionFit: A spree is a spell of unrestrained indulgence, like a binge.

clue.text: Favour one side on march — without good reason, clearly

parts.note: a limp favours one leg while walking

explanation.surface: A political side-taking on a protest march, done for no clear reason.
explanation.walkthrough: The march is a walk, and favouring one side is what an injured walker does.
explanation.definitionFit: Limpidly means in a clear, transparent way.

clue.text: Alarming colour after nap exercise class cured

parts.note: kip is British slang for a sleep
red is the colour of alarms

explanation.surface: Someone flushed a worrying colour after dozing, until an exercise class put them right.
explanation.walkthrough: Cured looks like 'healed', but it means preserved: a kipper is a smoked herring.
explanation.definitionFit: Kippered fish has been cured by salting and smoking.

clue.text: Bottle among others set out near tonic

indicators.note: the letters are laid out afresh

explanation.surface: A bottle placed with others next to the tonic water at a bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Among others' makes the definition fair: a bottle is just one of many kinds of container.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example, made honest by 'among others', since a bottle is only one kind.

clue.text: Often I meet Rob running rather late

indicators.note: the letters are set in motion

explanation.surface: Someone who keeps bumping into Rob when he is jogging, a bit behind schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: Rob looks like a verb, which hides that it is just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Not before time' is said of something that has come rather late.

clue.text: Quiet American turned chart over

indicators.note: turned round: read backwards

explanation.surface: The Quiet American, Graham Greene's novel, spun round on a chart.
explanation.walkthrough: The Quiet American is a Graham Greene novel, which glues the first two words together; they must be split.
explanation.definitionFit: RE- means again and 'over' means again, so charting over is mapping anew.

clue.text: Gold miners brought round mountain

indicators.note: turned round: read backwards

parts.note: the National Union of Mineworkers, the British miners' union

explanation.surface: Gold miners hauling their find round a mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: A Munro is a Scottish mountain over 3,000 feet.
explanation.definitionFit: A Munro is a Scottish mountain higher than 3,000 feet.

clue.text: Let out of wrong toilet, he left — just as she appeared

indicators.note: the letters are put wrong
to be let out of somewhere is to leave it, so the letters L-E-T leave the word

explanation.surface: A man let out of the wrong toilet, leaving just as a woman walked in.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening 'Let out of' belongs to 'left', at the far end of the wordplay, leaving only F.
explanation.definitionFit: A portrait done to the life shows the sitter exactly as she appeared.

clue.text: French teacher had me explain the merits of English

parts.note: had me do it = made me do it
to sell an idea is to explain its merits

explanation.surface: A pupil made to justify the value of English to their French teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: In British schools a female French teacher was traditionally addressed as Mademoiselle. 'French' does double duty, also putting 'me' into French.
explanation.definitionFit: Mademoiselle is how pupils addressed a woman teaching them French.

clue.text: Well, well — divorced by British rugby player

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise that a British rugby player has divorced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well, well' reads as one exclamation but gives two different meanings, a noun and an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The Springboks are South Africa's national rugby team.

clue.text: Racer with ordinary history shares concern, failing to finish

indicators.note: a word that fails to finish never reaches its end, so it loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A racing driver with an unremarkable past who is worried about not finishing.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is fair because a stock car started life as an ordinary production car before being modified for racing.
explanation.definitionFit: A stock car is a standard production car adapted for racing.

clue.text: Guerrillas struggle against leaders in the guard house

indicators.note: the leading letters of the following words

parts.note: first letters of the and guard
con = against, as in pros and cons

explanation.surface: Guerrillas fighting their way against the leaders held in a guardhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guard house' reads as one building, but house is the verb: the two initials house CON.
explanation.definitionFit: The Vietcong were the communist guerrillas of the Vietnam War.

clue.text: Maths book concealing fiddle on test

indicators.note: to conceal is to hide inside, so the book holds the other letters within it

parts.note: a tome is a large book
to rig is to fiddle a result

explanation.surface: A maths textbook hiding a cheat for an exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maths book' looks like a single textbook, but the definition stops at Maths and the book is only wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the study of triangles and angles is one branch of maths.

clue.text: Discarded bit of fruit upset bears when hibernating

indicators.note: in a down clue, set upside down: read upwards

parts.note: the peel is the part thrown away

explanation.surface: Bears in winter, dozing among the fruit scraps they have knocked over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bears' is a verb, not animals, though the surface uses the animals to make hibernating fit.
explanation.definitionFit: Hibernation is a long winter sleep, so the adjective fits as a near synonym.

clue.text: Fiat 500 king much appreciated when taken in it

parts.note: ta is British slang for thank you

explanation.surface: A Fiat 500 hatchback that a king adores and drives around.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fiat 500 is a small car, which welds '500' to 'Fiat'; fiat here is a decree.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonyms: both words, Latin and German borrowings, name a decree imposed by authority.

clue.text: Have larks avoided bitter berries?

parts.note: to cut someone or something is to avoid it
capers are sharp-tasting pickled buds and berries

explanation.surface: Birds steering clear of sour berries.
explanation.walkthrough: Larks look like birds eating berries, but 'have larks' means have fun.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for an idiom: a caper is a playful leap, and larks are pranks, both meaning to frolic.

clue.text: What flipping idiot has bagged barbecue leftovers?

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so the word is read backwards
to bag something is to put it in a bag, so one word holds the other

explanation.surface: An exasperated question about what some fool has pocketed from the barbecue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British swear word; it is the reversal of EH.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashes are what is left once a barbecue burns out.

clue.text: Issue of immigrants aboard dinghies insoluble, on reflection

indicators.note: the answer is carried inside the words
reflected: read backwards

explanation.surface: The migrant crossing in small boats described as an intractable problem.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'issue' as a political problem; here it means offspring.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nisei are American-born children of Japanese immigrants.

clue.text: Choice for suit perhaps set, hearts

parts.note: to clot is to set solid

explanation.surface: A card player picking a suit, perhaps hearts.
explanation.walkthrough: The cards in the surface mislead: the suit is clothing, and cloth is chosen for it.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by 'perhaps': picking the material is one choice made for a tailored suit.

clue.text: Lowest in society played bingo in case

indicators.note: the letters are played about with

explanation.surface: The poorest people in society played bingo, just in case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In case' looks like a container instruction, but it is simply LEST.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignoblest means lowest in rank, humblest.

clue.text: Newspaper customer possibly wanting substance rather than ad catalogue

indicators.note: choosing one thing rather than another means swapping it in, so the new letters take the old ones' place

parts.note: a reader is one kind of newspaper customer
the gist is the substance of something
AD in READER is swapped out

explanation.surface: A newspaper buyer who would prefer real content to advertisements.
explanation.walkthrough: The ad complaint in the surface is literal: the letters AD come out of READER.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both are official lists recording entries.

clue.text: Slide down deep hole? Never mind

parts.note: to ski is to slide down a slope
a pit is a deep hole

explanation.surface: Someone thinking of skiing into a crevasse, then dropping the idea.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the break between wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Skip it' and 'never mind' both dismiss a subject.
